narrative.text: Opens the Arabic version of WHO's position paper on BCG vaccine, explaining that the series advises Member States on vaccines used in large-scale immunization programmes and is aimed mainly at national public health officials and immunization managers. Its summary notes that tuberculosis is closely tied to poverty and worsened by HIV and drug resistance, and that BCG reliably protects children against TB meningitis and disseminated disease but does not prevent primary infection or reactivation, so it should be used optimally until new vaccines become available.
Notes that BCG's effects against leprosy and Buruli ulcer, and its use in treating bladder cancer, fall outside the scope of the position paper.

Describes the public health burden of tuberculosis, citing WHO's 2001 estimates of cases, new infections and deaths and the concentration of disease in developing countries and among children. It highlights the lethal combination of TB and HIV, especially in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South-East Asia; the reference footnotes at the end of the extracted text are garbled.

Explains how reactivated latent TB produces cavitary lung disease that spreads bacilli through coughed aerosols, and estimates how many people one infectious case infects yearly. It also covers genetic susceptibility, the share of disease caused by M. tuberculosis versus M. bovis (spread through infected milk), the members of the M. tuberculosis complex from which BCG derives, and environmental mycobacteria.

Covers the slow growth of M. tuberculosis in culture, diagnosis by sputum smear microscopy and the role of modern molecular and DNA fingerprinting techniques, including the 1998 sequencing of the bacterium's genome. It then turns to immunology, linking protection to Th1 T-cell responses and interferon-gamma activation of macrophages.

Continues the immunology of TB, describing the roles of CD8+ T cells, antibodies and Th2 responses, lifelong latency of the bacillus and reactivation linked to immune deficiency such as HIV. It explains that a positive tuberculin (Mantoux) skin test indicates delayed hypersensitivity rather than protection, and outlines the usually silent course of primary infection and its possible spread in young children.

Describes the clinical course of TB, from miliary disease and meningitis in children to latent infection that reactivates in 5–10% of people, along with classic symptoms and cavity formation in the lungs. It also covers bovine TB transmitted through unpasteurized milk, the basis of diagnosis including tuberculin testing, and the growing difficulty and cost of treating multidrug-resistant TB.

Argues that BCG, the only available TB vaccine, saves lives by protecting infants against TB meningitis and disseminated disease, though it does not stop primary infection or reactivation, and that TB control depends on combined case-finding, treatment and better vaccines. It then outlines the vaccine's history since 1921, its inclusion in the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1974, current coverage of about 100 million children a year, and the main strains in use.

States that no BCG strain has been shown to be superior and explains administration: intradermal injection, usually in the deltoid region, with reduced doses for newborns and possible co-administration with other childhood vaccines. It describes the usual local reaction and scar, vaccination schedules according to TB burden, and hypotheses for the variable protection observed between hot and cold regions, including exposure to environmental mycobacteria.

Reviews evidence on BCG efficacy from meta-analyses of trials and case-control studies, giving average protection rates against TB meningitis, disseminated TB, TB disease and TB death, particularly when vaccination is given at birth or in infancy. It notes the limited evidence for protection in adults, that revaccination does not boost immunity, and that protection wanes after 10–20 years.

States that BCG has almost no effect on TB transmission because it does not prevent reactivation of latent infection, then covers adverse events such as rare fatal disseminated BCG infection in severely immunocompromised people and local ulceration or lymphadenitis. It advises reduced doses for young infants and sets out cautions on vaccinating HIV-infected infants depending on symptoms and TB endemicity.

Describes the recent growth in experimental TB vaccine candidates, including recombinant BCG, attenuated M. tuberculosis strains, subunit and DNA vaccines, aimed at preventing infection, reactivation or relapse. It begins WHO's general position on vaccines and recommends giving BCG to newborns as soon as possible after birth in high-prevalence countries.

Completes WHO's position on BCG, recommending vaccination of all newborns in HIV-endemic high-burden areas but not of infants or children with symptomatic HIV, and allowing low-burden countries to target high-risk groups. It closes by framing TB control as a matter of equity and human rights and calls for sustained international support to develop safe, effective and affordable new vaccines.
